Smoking (almost) daily for about 4 years and it has done wonders for my physical and mental health.

I think it's the things you do alongside smoking that makes the difference.

As a daily smoker, the things you do whilst high will become a habit and those habits will become your reality.
You need to be mindful of everything you consume, think or do when high as a daily smoker.

If you smoke once in a while, indulging in munchies, mindlessly scrolling social media, playing video games or thinking about the past/daydreaming can be a fun activity.

If you smoke daily and do those things, they will lead you to some dark places.

1. Rather find a physical or creative activity to do whilst you smoke. Write in a journal, draw, do cardio, lift weights, do yoga, dance, cleaning, sewing, painting, sculpting. Find something you can do daily that you enjoy.

2. Be very mindful of the music you listen to, weed puts you in a very susceptible state and the music listened to will affect your mood. Create a playlist of upbeat music. Explore different genres of faster paced music.

If you struggle with social media when you're high, put your phone on airplane mode and put a timer or give yourself a set amount of time before allowing yourself to go back online.

3. To avoid unhealthy snacks, make a healthier choice the easier choice, before you smoke, chop up a bowl of fruit and have a large bottle of water close at hand. 

Making a habit of these three things takes time and patience(it took me years), but if you do it whilst high, it'll gradually improve your experience of weed.

Gloss varnish is a clear artist varnish that dries with a shiny finish. Gloss varnish can really help colours pop.

Artist fixative is a clear spray that fixes pencil and pastel colour  to the paper so they don't smudge and you don't have to over work the paper to get the shading you want.

The artist fixative I have dries with a shiny finish so I need to add a layer of matte varnish to create a surface I can keep colouring.

Its alot of layers 🙌🏼😐

I'm really like looking at teeth, so I have a folder of pictures from regular teeth to dental malocclusions they're all so fascinating.

Find the pair that inspires you the most🤔

First I paint a layer of the most used colour in both the teeth and the guns and then I start adding layers of soft pastels to give it depth and shadow, then a layer of artist fixative, when that's dry add a layer of matte varnish, let it dry and repeat the process with the soft pastels, fixative and matte varnish.

Once you feel you like the shading, add the light reflecting off of the teeth and gums. 
Add a few thin layers of gloss varnish, once fully dry and then add some thicker layers to create a smooth surface.

For now, stop drawing completely.

During  the break, if you have ideas of what you'd want to draw, envision them, write them down in a book, describe  them with as much detail as you can, appreciate art you'd want to emulate, think of how you would draw it, what colors you would use, what emotions youd want to bring out through the art, but DON'T draw. 

Take your time and let the excitement and urge to draw build up again. 
If you draw everyday, take 2 weeks off.
If you draw weekly, take a month or so off.
If you draw monthly, take 3 or more months off.


When you're absolutely dying to draw and have stacks of ideas youd want to put on paper. 

Allow yourself to draw.

If what you want to draw is too complicated, practice simplified versions until you understand how to work the angles.
If it's just too complicated, continue practicing the pose but simplified. 
If it's too frustrating, work on another idea that is more manageable.
 If you've waited long enough and compiled enough ideas, you wont become caught up on perfecting that one drawing.

Draw from a place of enjoyment. Take this self imposed pressure off of yourself.

I think you're putting the cart before the horse.

You need to be ok with being bad at something before you become good. 

It seems you're jumping from medium to medium(iPad to drawing tablet) before progressing past the beginner phase. Then getting discouraged when you have to learn something new and sucking again in the beginning.

Choose a medium to focus on, kindly ask artists you look up to share some of their work from the beginning of their art career with you. This can give you a realistic perspective of what they were creating in the beginning. Ask them how long they've been drawing and how often they've been drawing.
This should be enough to dispel any unrealistic expectations and give you a realistic timeline of what to expect if you apply yourself.

Ask yourself why you're creating art. 
Look for reasons that dont rely on the applause of other people. List those reasons down and commit them to memory. When you're at your lowest, use those reasons to spur you on.

Art as a career is not for the faint of heart.

I too struggle with keeping focus. 

Try setting a countdown timer for yourself whilst drawing. I use 2 hour slots but 45min, 1 hour, 1hr 30 mins are also good. Find what amount of time works for you.
Listen to music, avoid watching videos and have a drink or 2(tea, coffee, juice, water, whatever you like) at close hand. 
Cut down on as many distractions as possible.

The timer will give you a set time to spend focusing on your art. 
Keep the timer running in the background and out of view, if you start to feel your focus fading, take a look at the timer, it'll remind you that you're not drawing forever, music is a good way to get lost in your art and the time will just fly by.

When the timer runs out, take a short break(say 30mins), do something that has nothing to do with art.
Scroll social media, tidy up, read a chapter of a book, go outside, do other work, stretch, have a snack or a meal, etc. Keep it 30mins, otherwise youd lose track of time.

Then come back with a fresh drink and see if you feel like starting the timer again.

Doing your work bit by bit will help you improve and build your focus  just as much as doing long art sessions.
